correspondence.component_scope: Chosen eastern opening north of Corralitos
correspondence.finding: The actual selected eastern opening follows the westward drainage labeled A. Cruz Bonche on the El Salto original, north of Corralitos and west of the north–south Vaquería drainage and road. Its first bends and continuing western approach are visible in the original linework. The Vaquería course east of the opening is separate.

correspondence.component_scope: Western upper valley and northern bend
correspondence.finding: The chosen course continues west into the river explicitly labeled Río los Asientos, bends northwest through the deeply incised valley, and receives the separate northern Quebrada approach in the Los Frailes surroundings. The sequence then continues west and southwest, north of La Vinata del Cerro Prieto. The selected course is visible rather than inferred from basin membership.

correspondence.component_scope: Upper joining sector and El Palmar–La Escondida descent
correspondence.finding: The selected eastern approach descends southwest into the joining valley east of La Petaca and Cerro San Antonio. The topographic map distinguishes the northwestern approach labeled Río Palmito from the selected eastern Los Asientos approach. Below this joining sector the chosen route bends past El Palmar and receives the eastern Arroyo el Palmito approach, then follows the river directly labeled Río Baluarte west of La Escondida and east of Cuatantal.

correspondence.component_scope: Middle Baluarte canyon and eastern joining river
correspondence.finding: The continuous selected canyon proceeds south through successive bends along the Durango–Sinaloa boundary setting. Near Cerro San Cristóbal it receives the separately mapped river approaching from the Pueblo Nuevo/Agua Caliente direction; that eastern approach is also labeled Río Baluarte on the state original. The selected northern approach and the connected receiving trunk remain distinguishable. Both originals expose the intermediate joins and southward continuation toward the Santa María surroundings.

correspondence.component_scope: Santa María–La Guamuchiltita continuation
correspondence.finding: Repeated Baluarte inscriptions identify the selected southern canyon approaching Santa María, including the eastern Arroyo Plomosas joining setting on the state sheet. The topographic original then continues the selected river past La Guamuchiltita and Potrero de los Laureles toward Matatán. The historical maps establish the corridor and ordinary joins. They do not establish the subsequent Santa María storage configuration or current open-water boundaries.

correspondence.component_scope: Matatán storage passage and western outlet
correspondence.finding: West of Matatán, the El Salto original shows the named blue waterbody Gerardo Estrada and its western dam symbol beside Hacienda el Tamarindo. The original hydrography legend distinguishes the dam/impoundment symbol from ordinary river and canal linework. The selection enters from the northern Baluarte approach, crosses this mapped storage reach, and continues below its western outlet. The separate Río Matatán approaches from the southeast. This is a distinct mapped impoundment passage rather than an exposed river reach throughout.

correspondence.component_scope: Copales bend, Pánuco join and El Rosario
correspondence.finding: Below the mapped Gerardo Estrada outlet, the selected course turns northwest by Copales and then southwest along Loma Blanca into El Rosario. The maps separately show Río Pánuco arriving from the north through Cacalotán and joining this lower Baluarte corridor. The selected impoundment outlet and Baluarte approach are not replaced by the northern Pánuco branch. The two originals overlap through the western lowland and El Rosario setting.

correspondence.component_scope: El Rosario–El Pozole–Chametla lower river
correspondence.finding: The state original continues the same channel southwest from El Rosario through Laguna de Beltranes and the Nieblas–El Pozole surroundings, then toward Chametla and Boca de Río. River linework is distinguished from the highways, railway and the straighter managed waterways farther east near La Reforma. The selection remains on the lower river corridor.

correspondence.component_scope: Actual selected Pacific terminal at Boca de Río/Majahual
correspondence.finding: The last selected southwestward approach corresponds to the lower channel at Boca de Río and Majahual, where the original river line reaches the Pacific coastal margin. Laguna el Caimanero lies separately to the northwest and Laguna Grande with its wetland channels lies southeast of the chosen outlet. Neither lagoon is substituted for this terminal or assigned as a selected lake crossing. The western coastal approach is visible in the original map.

correspondence.component_scope: Selected northwestern opening and Itororó approach
correspondence.finding: The municipal original depicts the chosen northwest-to-southeast river corridor through Cabeceira do Colônia and São José do Colônia into the Itororó/Bandeira do Colônia setting, with Rio Colônia printed on the watercourse. The regional original overlaps this opening and its continuation. Intermittent upper-channel symbols are source observations, not a claim of present flow or a surveyed river-source point.

correspondence.component_scope: Itororó eastward course and Rio do Meio join
correspondence.finding: The municipal sheet traces Colônia east from Itororó along the southern boundary corridor through the Sobradinho/Oriente and Porto Alegre settings. Rio do Meio descends from the north and joins the selected river farther east. The regional sheet overlaps this connection; the separate Rio do Meio approach is not substituted for the selected Colônia course.

correspondence.component_scope: Middle Colônia bends to Itaju do Colônia
correspondence.finding: The regional original follows the eastward and southeastern bends, the southern Agua Vermelha tributary setting and the turn toward Itaju do Colônia. The main channel then turns northeast. The EIA regional map independently places this connected Colônia course between Itororó and Itaju do Colônia.

correspondence.component_scope: Northeast Colônia and the Estiva dam-project corridor
correspondence.finding: EIA figures 3.1 and 3.2 depict the selected Colônia valley entering the elongated planned reservoir northeast of Itaju do Colônia, passing the impoundment corridor and continuing below the proposed dam near Estiva toward Itapé. The project river and outlet join are visible; the proposed BA-120 relocation is a separate road line. The 2011 report explicitly marks the dam as a project, so neither present construction nor operating state or current reservoir shoreline is inferred.

correspondence.component_scope: Salgado junction and Itapé continuation
correspondence.finding: The regional map shows Colônia arriving from the southwest and Salgado from the west/northwest near Itapé, with the selected continuation turning east and northeast. EIA printed page 36 explicitly identifies Cachoeira as the river formed by the Colônia–Salgado junction upstream of Itapé. This supports the named transition without assigning an exact name-boundary vertex.

correspondence.component_scope: Ferradas, Piabanha junction and Itabuna
correspondence.finding: The originals follow the receiving river past the separate Piabanha contribution and Ferradas into Itabuna. EIA figure 3.1 and its prose distinguish the existing-at-publication level-dam/intake setting and water-supply infrastructure from the continuing river. No selected aqueduct shortcut, present operating status or precise individual structure crossing is asserted.

correspondence.component_scope: Itabuna to lower Cachoeira
correspondence.finding: The regional original labels Cachoeira east of Itabuna and depicts its successive bends along the BR-415 corridor, the southern Jacarecica contribution and the widening lower channel west of Ilhéus. The EIA situation map provides an overlapping river connection between Itabuna and Ilhéus.

correspondence.component_scope: Actual selected terminal continuation at Ilhéus
correspondence.finding: The inspected regional map follows the west-entry Cachoeira channel into the connected broad estuary, with Fundão joining from the north and Santana from the south and an open connection to the Atlantic beside Ilhéus/Pontal. EIA printed page 36 independently describes this combined estuary and ocean outlet. The selected final eastward then northward continuation ends in the northern Ilhéus estuary/city-edge setting; the regional cartography does not place that generalized endpoint as an exact open-sea or shoreline vertex. The terminal waterbody and its through-connection are established at ordinary estuarine scale, with no claim of exact bank agreement or a distinct name for every estuarine branch.

correspondence.component_scope: Actual southeastern chosen opening and northwestern upper valley
correspondence.finding: M-1 and M-24 depict the southeastern Perejil stem at and beyond the selected opening, followed continuously north-northwest into the upper valley. Nearby small lakes lie outside the selected channel; no lake-crossing connector is asserted.

correspondence.component_scope: Upper northwest-to-west bend and Río Grande reach
correspondence.finding: The same mapped blue watercourse turns west-northwest through the Río Grande-labelled valley. Its relation to the Agua Blanca and Huaranchal side drainage is exposed. These labels distinguish tributaries and do not transfer their names to the selected trunk.

correspondence.component_scope: Northwest-trending receiving valley and Huancay approach
correspondence.finding: M-1 and M-24 continue the selected trunk past the mapped Succhabamba and adjoining side-drainage setting into the Huancay-labelled northwestern approach. The watercourse remains connected through all selected joins. No exact local boundary between the Grande and Huancay names is assigned.

correspondence.component_scope: Chuquillanqui confluence, western arc and middle receiving course
correspondence.finding: The map visibly joins the Huancay approach to the separate northeastern Río Chuquillanqui branch. The selected course takes the receiving western arc, then the southwestward course below the northern Ochape/Cascas drainage. The unselected Chuquillanqui branch is not included in the representative scalar.

correspondence.component_scope: Southward middle descent, Quirripano junction and western lower-valley turn
correspondence.finding: M-1 and M-19 expose the southward receiving channel, the separate eastern Quirripano contribution and the selected westward turn south of Ascope. The lower multichannel valley is continuous with the mapped Chicama receiving course at ordinary corridor scale.

correspondence.component_scope: Southwest lower Chicama corridor and actual coastal terminal
correspondence.finding: The selected final southwest approach follows the explicitly labelled Río Chicama corridor to the mapped Pacific coastline. M-1 and M-19 expose the entire terminal reach and coastal outlet, rather than merely a basin boundary or inland label. Individual lower-channel banks are not resolved or required.

correspondence.component_scope: Chosen western opening and upper West Fork San Jacinto River
correspondence.finding: The selected opening west of Loma lies on the mapped West Fork San Jacinto River corridor. The named channel runs northeast, turns east through the wooded wetland valley past the Rocky Creek and Era Branch joining settings, then bends south near Chandlers Way. The opening is not asserted to be the ultimate or officially designated river source. Original channels, their joins and repeated labels support the corridor rather than labels alone.

correspondence.component_scope: Upper West Fork southward trunk and Lake Conroe inflow
correspondence.finding: The connected named river crosses the State Highway 30 setting, continues south past the Welch Branch and Casidy Branch joining settings, and receives West Sandy Creek and McDonald Creek near Bath. It widens into the northern reservoir arm through the Sam Houston National Forest, past the East Sandy Creek and Caney Creek joining settings and the FM1375 crossing. The named river arm connects to the open water mapped as Lake Conroe.

correspondence.component_scope: Lake Conroe passage and dam outlet
correspondence.finding: The selected passage lies within the continuous northern arm and main Lake Conroe waterbody, continuing south across the FM1097 bridge setting to its southern dam. The map depicts the outlet into the labelled West Fork San Jacinto River beside Magnolia Lake and its continuation across State Highway 105. This establishes the ordinary reservoir-to-river connection; no present release, gate state, water level or operational claim is made.

correspondence.component_scope: Conroe and the middle West Fork corridor
correspondence.finding: The named river continues past Leonidas, the Egypt Creek setting and the west side of Conroe. It receives Lake Creek, passes the Grand Lake surroundings, crosses I45, continues through the Stewarts Creek and Little Caney Creek joining settings, and runs past Woodloch and the State Highway 242 crossing. The selected line remains on this trunk; nearby floodplain lakes and tributaries are not substituted as river names.

correspondence.component_scope: Lower West Fork through Porter Heights and Kingwood
correspondence.finding: Repeated West Fork San Jacinto River labels and continuous water features trace the valley past the Sleepy Hollow and Porter Heights surroundings, the Grand Parkway crossing, Lake Branch, Black Slough and Woods Gully. The river receives Spring Creek near Kingwood, crosses the US59/I69 setting, then turns east through the lower San Jacinto River corridor north of Humble and Atascocita. The map depicts its continuous entry into Lake Houston. Tributary joining settings are distinguished from the selected trunk.

correspondence.component_scope: Lake Houston passage and dam outlet
correspondence.finding: The selected lower-river arm enters the connected northern Lake Houston waterbody near Lake Houston Parkway and Scotts Point. The map labels this waterbody with both the river and reservoir names in their respective settings. The continuous lake extends south through the FM1960 crossing and Atascocita–Huffman surroundings to the southern dam; its outlet channel continues into the San Jacinto River at the Big Eddy setting. Ordinary inflow, through-reservoir and outlet correspondence are established without inferring current operations.

correspondence.component_scope: Lower San Jacinto River and tidal widening
correspondence.finding: The mapped river continues below Lake Houston through Big Eddy, Magnolia Gardens, the Jackson Bayou joining setting, the Beaumont Highway and US90 crossings, and the Muleshoe Lake, Heads Bend and George White Lake surroundings. It turns east and south past Highlands, then broadens through Grennel Slough and Diamond Island toward the I10 crossing at Gilbert Landing and Four Corners Lynchburg. These are connected mapped water features; adjacent named lakes retain their separate local identities.

correspondence.component_scope: Actual selected terminal in the Lynchburg–Brownwood inner tidal setting
correspondence.finding: The actual rendered endpoint lies beside Brownwood in the inner tidal water complex southeast of Four Corners Lynchburg, rather than at an outer Galveston Bay or Gulf mouth. Original cartography depicts a broad receiving-water connection from the I10 river reach around the Lynchburg peninsula into the Brownwood-side open water. The long straight final model extension cuts across local Four Corners/Lynchburg land and shoreline before reaching that water and the Brownwood edge. It is a generalized terminal depiction, not an all-water channel trace. No unestablished distinct waterbody or interbasin transfer is needed to associate the selected terminal with this continuously mapped receiving-water complex at ordinary corridor scale. Exact banks, artificial shore structures and tidal channels are not assigned.
